> >
> > A) How can I export (and into which program?) the detection function
> > graph? Is it possible to construct it in Excel or Adobe Illustrator?

In the D4 results browser, go to the plot so it is on the screen and then
select the menu item Analysis Results and choose Copy Plot to Clipboard.
In word or another package, use Paste or Paste Special - Picture.

> >

> > B) As I am using Whitesides (1987?) method of establishing the
> > perpendicular distance to the center of the primate group - by
> > incorporating average group spread and adding 1/2 of that to the
> > perpendicular distance measured from line to the first primate - there
> > is a new source of error which is added(=group spread). (I understand
> > that the method has some draw backs, however it proved most practical
> > in dense vegetation.) HOW can I incorporate the variation and its
> > standard error in DISTANCE. I have been trying to add it as a
> > multiplier, but I have not managed to keep track of the analysis in
> > that way and so feel unsure about the results.
> >

The error you are describing is measurement error in the distances and
there is currently no way to include that source of error with the
software. A multiplier would not be appropriate.

> >A) How can I export (and into which program?) the detection function
> >graph? Is it possible to construct it in Excel or Adobe Illustrator?

Jeff's answer is quite correct, and you could have saved him the trouble of
answering you by pressing F1 in Distance, and then looking in the online help
index under "Copy | Results to other programs".

In addition, if you had searched the online archives of the distance-sampling
list (available from within Distance by choosing "Help | Distance on the web |
distance-sampling list archive", using the key words "plot" or "Excel" with the
substring search button ticked, you would have found the message titled
"ANNOUNCE: Excel macro for Distance g(x) plots". This macro (written by Tim
Gerrodette) takes the numbers produced when you paste a plot into excel using
"paste" rather than "paste special" and turns them back into a plot which you
can then customize. The macro is available from the "Distance Support, Updates
and Extras" page of the Distance web site. It was originally written for
Distance 3.5, but I expect it will work fine for Distance 4 plots too (although
I haven't tried it). If it doesn't work please contact me and I'll fix it up.

My general point here is please check all available sources of information
before posting to the list.

> >B) As I am using Whitesides (1987?) method of establishing the
> >perpendicular distance to the center of the primate group - by
> >incorporating average group spread and adding 1/2 of that to the
> >perpendicular distance measured from line to the first primate - there
> >is a new source of error which is added(=group spread). (I understand
> >that the method has some draw backs, however it proved most practical
> >in dense vegetation.) HOW can I incorporate the variation and its
> >standard error in DISTANCE. I have been trying to add it as a
> >multiplier, but I have not managed to keep track of the analysis in
> >that way and so feel unsure about the results.

Aha - now this was a valid question! Again Dr Distance (Jeff) was quite right
that it's a measurement error and can't be addressed directly in Distance. The
only solution I can think of if you have access to someone who can program is to
write a little simulation program that creates samples from your original data
like a regular bootstrap but also adding in the measurement error (i.e., adding
in random values drawn from the distribution of group spread), runs Distance
from the command line (see online help about this) and extracts the results --
repeat this many times to incorporate the uncertainty in distances.

We have a student here, Tiago Marques, who is interested in measurement error,
so I'm cc'ing this to him to see if he can think of anything more practical
(he's away for much of the summer so it will likely be a while before you hear
from him).

One approach would be to guesstimate how big the effect of such measurement
errors might be. One way to categorize measurement error is as either additive
(the error is added to the true distances) or multiplicative (the error
multiplies or divides the true distance). I haven't read the Whiteside paper
you refer to, but from what you said it seems you have additive errors -- you
add in 1/2 the group spread estimate. There's a paper by Song Chen (1998) in
Biometrics that looks at additive errors, with some results summarized on page
264 of Introduction to Distance sampling: "Chen (1998) showed that the expected
bias was a function of the error magnitude and the width of the shoulder of the
detection function (i.e. values of x such that g(x) is approximately 1). When
the standard deviation of the measurement errors was approximately one-half the
width of the detection function shoulder, the expected bias in density was less
than -3%." This addresses any possible bias caused by the measurement error; I
don't remember if Song also looked at the increase in variance caused by the
additional source of uncertainty.

Hope this helps a little!

- Len

Kristina,

Here's a suggestion, but not a definative answer -- others may have other
suggestions/ideas:

You could use %native as a covariate in a multiple covariate analysis (MCDS
analysis engine). This allows the scale of the detection function to vary as %
native varies. Then predict density for each point (under Model Definition |
Estimate tick the Density by sample box). Get these predicted densities out of
Distance and into some other stats package, and do a regression of estimated
density against percentage of native habitat at each point. Since density is
(at least close to) log-normally distributed (Introduction to Distance page 77)
you may want to log-transform the densities before doing the regression -- you
can then assume errors are normally distributed. As a refinement, you could
weight each density by its estimated CV if they are very different between
points (unlikely).

For getting the density estimates out of distance, you could do it manually
(i.e., type the estimates into a stats package) or if you have the skill you
could write a little program to parse the stats file that Distance can output
with each run (look in the online help Index under "Saving CDS analysis results
| Saving to file").

By the way, can I remind people to use appropriate subject lines when they post
to the list -- we've had two postings in one day with no subject line - this
makes it hard for people to follow up any replies and find messages in the
archive. A suggested subject for this post might be "Question: differences
between habitats". For more on this, see point 2 of the list guidelines at
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/files/DISTANCE-SAMPLING/distance-sampling.welcome

Cheers,

- Len
